sections.h2: Does New Jersey tax the gain when I sell my house?
sections.html:
Yes. New Jersey treats gain on a home sale as income and calculates it the same way the federal return does, so any amount taxable federally is taxable in the state. The Division's guide routes the gain through the same return as your other income, for the year of the sale (NJ Division of Taxation home guide).

The basic math is the sale price minus your adjusted basis, which starts with what you paid and moves with improvements. For a house you inherited, the IRS points to Publication 551 for basis rules instead of using the original owner's purchase price. A loss on a personal residence is not deductible, according to the IRS.

The state's top bracket matters for large gains. New Jersey raised its Gross Income Tax rate to 10.75 percent on income above $1 million beginning with tax year 2020, and a big sale can push a seller into that bracket in a single year.

sections.h2: Who can exclude the gain on a New Jersey home sale?
sections.html:
A principal residence owner can shelter up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, after passing the ownership and use tests. New Jersey follows the federal exclusion, and it applies whether you stay in the state or move away.

  • Ownership test: you owned the home for two or more years during the five years ending on the sale date.
  • Use test: you lived in it as your main home for two or more years in that same five year window.
  • Additional home test: you did not exclude gain on another home sale during the two years before this sale.
  • A joint filing couple reaches $500,000 only if both pass the use test, and a couple where just one spouse qualifies is held to $250,000.

Sellers who miss the two year mark because of a job change, health problem or unforeseen event may claim a reduced exclusion. The IRS also says you must report the sale when you receive a Form 1099-S, even if all of the gain is excludable (IRS Topic 701). Rental properties, second homes and vacation homes do not count as a principal residence.

sections.h2: What changes if the gain is above the exclusion?
sections.html:
The excess is a capital gain, and federal rates depend on how long you held the house. Gain on a home held one year or less is short term and taxed as ordinary income. Longer holds get lower rates, which for tax years beginning in 2025 were 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on taxable income (IRS Topic 409).

The IRS lists a few extras that sellers of residential property sometimes run into. The portion of any unrecaptured section 1250 gain is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent, and people with significant investment income may owe the net investment income tax. You report the sale on Form 8949 and Schedule D of the federal return.

New Jersey adds its own filing steps. Residents report the gain on Schedule B of the NJ-1040 as Net Gains or Income From Disposition of Property. Nonresidents use Part I of the NJ-1040-NR. If the sale produced a loss, the state form takes a zero on that line.

sections.h2: Do I owe New Jersey tax at the closing table?
sections.html:
Only if you are a nonresident, and every seller still files a GIT/REP form to record the deed. A seller who keeps a New Jersey residence files form GIT/REP-3 at closing, which exempts the estimated payment. The tax on any gain is then settled with the NJ-1040 the following filing season.

A New Jersey resident who sells and moves out of state counts as a nonresident for this sale. A nonresident must send an estimated payment of either 2 percent of the consideration or 8.97 percent of the net gain, before or at closing, unless a seller's assurance on GIT/REP-3 applies. The check is made out to the State of New Jersey, Division of Taxation, and travels with the paperwork to the settlement agent.

sections.h2: Which GIT/REP exemptions are common, and who signs?
sections.html:
The person who signs the deed completes and signs the form, either the seller or an authorized representative holding a power of attorney or a letter of authority. Each owner files, married and civil union couples count as one owner, and an estate or trust files a single form that can carry several trustee or executor signatures.

  • The seller is a New Jersey resident.
  • Total consideration is $1,000 or less.
  • The seller is a business entity.
  • The seller is a nonresident claiming the principal residence exclusion.

Only sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales avoid the form entirely. A county clerk can still reject a deed for reasons outside the Division's control. The Division suggests printing its instructions, highlighting the relevant passage and showing it to the clerk before escalating (GIT/REP FAQs).

sections.h2: How do I get back an overpaid estimated payment?
sections.html:
A nonresident seller can file Form A-3128 after closing to claim an early refund of an overpayment. The Division wants proof such as the settlement statement or closing disclosure. The form does not replace the NJ-1040-NR, which must still be filed for the year the property sold, and the final refund comes out of that return.

Because the 2 percent and 8.97 percent figures are estimates, a seller who took a small gain or a loss often overpays. Keep the closing disclosure, the deed, and records of improvements together so the return is easy to prepare.

sections.h2: What records should a New Jersey seller keep for the return?
sections.html:
Keep the paperwork that proves your basis and the closing numbers, because the gain is figured on the return and not at the table. A nonresident who sold must file the NJ-1040-NR for the year the property was sold, and the closing payment is listed on the estimated payment line.

  • The settlement statement or closing disclosure from the purchase and from the sale.
  • Receipts for capital improvements. The Division notes that New Jersey does not allow certain federal deductions such as mortgage interest or capital improvements on the NJ-1040, so these receipts matter for basis and not for a deduction.
  • The signed GIT/REP form and any payment receipt.
  • For an inherited house, the paperwork showing its value when the owner died. IRS Publication 551 covers inherited basis.

Estates and trusts complete one GIT/REP form, and it can carry signatures from more than one executor or trustee. Ask the estate's tax preparer how the sale is reported on the estate's own return.

faqs.q: Does New Jersey have its own capital gains tax for a home sale?
faqs.a: No separate tax exists. The state taxes the gain through its Gross Income Tax and follows the federal calculation, so a federally taxable amount is also taxable here.

faqs.q: What is the exclusion limit for spouses who sell together?
faqs.a: Spouses filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000 once the tests are met. When only one of them qualifies, the cap falls to $250,000.

faqs.q: Do I pay an estimated tax at closing if I stay in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. A resident who remains in the state submits form GIT/REP-3 and pays any income tax when filing the NJ-1040.

faqs.q: What happens if I sell and move to another state?
faqs.a: You are treated as a nonresident for the sale. Expect an estimated payment of 2 percent of the consideration or 8.97 percent of the net gain unless an exemption applies, plus an NJ-1040-NR the next year.

faqs.q: Which return reports the sale for a nonresident?
faqs.a: Form NJ-1040-NR, Part I, as Net Gains or Income From Disposition of Property, with any closing payment listed as an estimated payment, not as withholding.
